title: When do you use OkHttp `MockWebServer` (a real local HTTP server to test outbound `WebClient`/`RestClient` calls: verify request method/path/headers, simulate 404/500/timeout/retry) versus `WebTestClient` (in-memory, for testing your own reactive controllers with `@WebFluxTest` + `@MockBean`)?
shortTitle: When to use OkHttp MockWebServer versus WebTestClient: testing outbound HTTP calls versus testing your own reactive controllers
keyPoints: MockWebServer tests outbound calls your service makes to downstream services; WebTestClient tests inbound requests your own controllers receive.
MockWebServer is a real HTTP server on a local port: you enqueue scripted responses and assert the exact request your code sent.
MockWebServer shines at simulating downstream failure: 500s for retry logic, 404s for exception mapping, delays for timeout verification.
WebTestClient with @WebFluxTest loads only the web layer, mocks service collaborators, and verifies routing, validation, and response serialization.
The two are complementary, not competing: use both in the same test suite for different seams.
Choosing the wrong tool is a classic mistake: MockWebServer tells you nothing about your routing; WebTestClient tells you nothing about your outbound client.

s1_definition.oneliner: MockWebServer tests the outbound calls your service makes to downstream services; WebTestClient tests the inbound requests your own controllers receive.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **MockWebServer** – a real, lightweight HTTP server from OkHttp that binds to a local port; you enqueue scripted responses, point your outbound client at it, and assert the exact request sent.
- **WebTestClient** – an in-memory test client for your own inbound endpoints, used with `@WebFluxTest` and `@MockBean` to verify routing, validation, and response serialization.
- **Direction rule** – if the thing under test calls OUT to another service, use MockWebServer; if the thing under test receives INBOUND requests, use WebTestClient.
- **Complementary** – both are used in the same test suite for different seams: MockWebServer at the back door, WebTestClient at the front door.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's payments service as a bank teller. MockWebServer is a fake phone line pretending to be the credit bureau: you listen to exactly what the teller says and control what the bureau replies (testing outgoing calls). WebTestClient is playing the customer who walks up to the teller's counter with a transfer form: you verify the teller validates it, rejects bad forms, and processes good ones (testing incoming requests).

sections.s6_takeaway:
MockWebServer and WebTestClient solve opposite problems. MockWebServer is a real HTTP server you point your outbound client at to test the calls your service makes to downstream services: you enqueue scripted responses, verify the exact request your code sent, and simulate failure like 500s, 404s, and timeouts. WebTestClient drives your own inbound endpoints with `@WebFluxTest` and mocked collaborators to verify routing, validation, status codes, and response serialization.

The one-line rule is that MockWebServer tests outbound calls and WebTestClient tests inbound calls. The classic mistake is swapping them: using WebTestClient to test outbound resilience tells you nothing about your client, and using MockWebServer to test your routing tells you nothing about your endpoints.

At National Bank of India, our loan-eligibility service calls an external credit bureau that is flaky and costs money per call. We used MockWebServer to simulate bureau failures and verify retry and timeout behavior, and WebTestClient to verify our eligibility endpoint handles validation and returns the correct decisions. For full end-to-end slices we combined both: WebTestClient at the front door and MockWebServer at the back.

Remember one sentence: the direction of the call decides the tool: MockWebServer for outbound to faked downstreams, WebTestClient for inbound to your own controllers.
